headline: High risk: Windsurf’s shell/MCP/auto-execute defaults can amplify Copilot outputs into unsafe actions and data exposure.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Copilot has no shell or MCP, but it writes edits into open buffers and repo context, while Windsurf can ingest clipboard/files and use MCP. If Copilot-generated content is copied or saved into shared workspace files, Windsurf may treat attacker-controlled text as actionable. The shared filesystem bridge makes injection plausible, though not guaranteed by default.
conditions: IF Copilot output is copied into a file or buffer that Windsurf reads
IF Windsurf MCP tools parse that content as instructions
mitigations: Disable clipboard-based handoff between editors
Keep Copilot and Windsurf on separate workspaces
Require manual review before Windsurf tool calls
Use a read-only staging file for any cross-agent text

B_data_leakage.rationale: Copilot touches open editor buffers and repo context with vendor-only egress, while Windsurf reads workspace files, uses clipboard, and has broad network egress plus MCP. In a shared workspace, sensitive code or secrets in files can flow into both agents’ contexts and then out through Windsurf’s broader outbound paths. This is a default-configuration exposure pathway, not merely unusual setup.
conditions: IF both agents open the same repository or workspace
IF sensitive material is present in files or open buffers
IF Windsurf sends workspace context to external model/MCP endpoints
mitigations: Remove secrets from the shared workspace
Use separate repos or clones per agent
Turn off Windsurf auto-context sharing where possible
Restrict Copilot to non-sensitive files only

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Both agents can write the filesystem and modify git state; Windsurf also shares state via local filesystem and can auto-execute terminal commands, while Copilot can propose edits in Workspace. Concurrent edits to the same repo can race on git state and files, causing lost work or conflicting commits. The overlap is dangerous by default because neither profile shows locking or coordination.
conditions: IF both agents operate on the same git checkout
IF Windsurf auto-execute is enabled or terminal commands are approved
IF both agents modify overlapping files or branches
mitigations: Use separate branches per agent
Pause one agent before the other writes
Disable Windsurf auto-execute
Commit after each agent’s turn
requires-engineering: add file/branch locking in the orchestrator

D_cascading_error.rationale: Copilot’s Workspace plans and edits can become inputs to Windsurf’s agentic loop, and Windsurf can then execute commands or apply further changes. Because Windsurf has tool use and auto-execute capability, unverified Copilot output can cascade into real actions. The pair lacks a documented verification barrier in the profiles, so uncertainty pushes severity upward.
conditions: IF Windsurf consumes Copilot-generated edits or summaries as authoritative
IF Windsurf auto-execute is enabled or commands are approved without review
mitigations: Require human verification before Windsurf acts on Copilot output
Insert a diff review step between agents
Disable auto-execute in Windsurf
Limit Copilot to suggestion-only mode for critical files

E_compliance.rationale: Both agents are closed-source and touch source code/open files, but only Windsurf explicitly handles model provider keys and has broad egress; Copilot uses GitHub vendor-only egress. If regulated data or secrets are present in the workspace, differing retention and outbound paths can create compliance mismatch. The profiles do not prove a specific residency violation, so medium is the highest supportable level.
conditions: IF regulated data or secrets are stored in the shared workspace
IF organizational policy forbids sending that data to vendor or model-proxy services
mitigations: Exclude regulated files from both tools
Rotate any exposed keys immediately
Use a policy gate for sensitive paths
Document retention and residency settings before use
